techniques.name: SHapley Additive exPlanations
techniques.description: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) explains one prediction by sharing out the gap between that prediction and a baseline, usually the model's average output over a background dataset, among the input features. Each feature receives a signed score, where positive means it pushed the prediction above the baseline and negative means it pushed it below. The scores are Shapley values from game theory, meaning each is the feature's average effect over every order in which the features could be added, and together they add up exactly to the gap. Exact calculation is costly, so tools usually estimate the scores by sampling or use shortcuts for particular model types, such as a fast exact method for tree ensembles, and averaging the absolute scores over many predictions gives a global ranking of features. In a fairness use, the difference in average output between two groups is shared out feature by feature in the same way, showing which inputs account for the gap.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing a customer churn prediction model to understand why a specific high-value customer was flagged as likely to leave, revealing that recent support ticket interactions and declining purchase frequency were the main drivers.

A lender's model validation team investigates why a loan approval model approves one applicant group less often than another. They compute SHAP values for every applicant, compare the group averages feature by feature, and see which inputs, such as postcode or credit history length, account for most of the gap, so they know what to scrutinise first.

limitations.description: Common estimators fill in a 'missing' feature by sampling its value independently of the others. With correlated features, such as income and postcode, the model is then evaluated on unrealistic combinations and credit can be split between correlated features in ways that mislead. Check feature correlations before reading individual scores.

Exact values need the model evaluated on every subset of features, which grows exponentially with the number of features. Sampling estimators trade accuracy for speed, and explaining many predictions from a slow model, or a model with hundreds of features, can take hours. Tree ensembles have a much faster exact algorithm.

Scores are relative to a baseline set by the background dataset, and a different background gives different scores. Explaining an applicant against all customers says something different from explaining them against previously approved customers, so the choice must be made on purpose and reported.

SHAP describes what the model has learned, not how the world works. A large contribution does not show that changing that feature would change the real outcome, so the scores should not be used to advise people on what to change.

Averaging absolute scores into a global ranking can hide features that matter a great deal for a small subgroup, or that push in opposite directions for different people. Inspect the spread of per-prediction scores, not only the mean.

resources.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
resources.abstract: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

resources.title: From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees
resources.abstract: Tree-based machine learning models such as random forests, decision trees and gradient boosted trees are popular nonlinear predictive models, yet comparatively little attention has been paid to explaining their predictions. Here we improve the interpretability of tree-based models through three main contributions. (1) A polynomial time algorithm to compute optimal explanations based on game theory. (2) A new type of explanation that directly measures local feature interaction effects. (3) A new set of tools for understanding global model structure based on combining many local explanations of each prediction. We apply these tools to three medical machine learning problems and show how combining many high-quality local explanations allows us to represent global structure while retaining local faithfulness to the original model. These tools enable us to (1) identify high-magnitude but low-frequency nonlinear mortality risk factors in the US population, (2) highlight distinct population subgroups with shared risk characteristics, (3) identify nonlinear interaction effects among risk factors for chronic kidney disease and (4) monitor a machine learning model deployed in a hospital by identifying which features are degrading the model’s performance over time. Given the popularity of tree-based machine learning models, these improvements to their interpretability have implications across a broad set of domains. Tree-based machine learning models are widely used in domains such as healthcare, finance and public services. The authors present an explanation method for trees that enables the computation of optimal local explanations for individual predictions, and demonstrate their method on three medical datasets.

Explainable machine-learning predictions for the prevention of hypoxaemia during surgery
resources.abstract: Although anaesthesiologists strive to avoid hypoxaemia during surgery, reliably predicting future intraoperative hypoxaemia is not possible at present. Here, we report the development and testing of a machine-learning-based system that predicts the risk of hypoxaemia and provides explanations of the risk factors in real time during general anaesthesia. The system, which was trained on minute-by-minute data from the electronic medical records of over 50,000 surgeries, improved the performance of anaesthesiologists by providing interpretable hypoxaemia risks and contributing factors. The explanations for the predictions are broadly consistent with the literature and with prior knowledge from anaesthesiologists. Our results suggest that if anaesthesiologists currently anticipate 15% of hypoxaemia events, with the assistance of this system they could anticipate 30%, a large portion of which may benefit from early intervention because they are associated with modifiable factors. The system can help improve the clinical understanding of hypoxaemia risk during anaesthesia care by providing general insights into the exact changes in risk induced by certain characteristics of the patient or procedure. An alert system based on machine learning and trained on surgical data from electronic medical records helps anaesthesiologists prevent hypoxaemia during surgery by providing interpretable real-time predictions.

techniques.name: Permutation Importance
techniques.description: Permutation Importance measures how much a trained model relies on each input feature. For each feature, the values in a dataset are shuffled at random, which breaks the link between that feature and the outcome, and the model is scored again. The fall in score, for example in accuracy, is the feature's importance: a large fall means the model depends on the feature, and little or no fall means it does not. Repeating the shuffle several times shows how much the result varies. The method works with any model, but it shows what the model uses, not what causes the outcome in the world.

example_use_cases.description: Assessing which patient characteristics (e.g., age, blood pressure, cholesterol) matter most to a medical diagnosis model by shuffling each one in turn on held-out patients and recording the drop in performance, so a clinician can judge whether the model relies on clinically relevant factors.

A bank's model-risk team shuffles each input to a card-fraud model in turn on held-out transactions, to check the model leans on transaction behaviour and not on a field that leaks the answer, such as a case-handling code recorded after fraud was confirmed.

A flood-forecasting team shuffles each rainfall, river-level and soil-moisture input of a model trained on historic data, to check that forecasts depend on the physical drivers hydrologists expect and not on a calendar variable.

limitations.description: When features are strongly correlated, shuffling one leaves the model able to rely on its correlated partner, so both can show low importance even though the model uses them. Shuffling also creates feature combinations that do not occur in real data, which can distort the scores.

Computationally expensive for large datasets or complex models. The model is scored once per feature per shuffle, so cost grows with the number of features, the number of repeats and the size of the evaluation data. No retraining is needed.

The score for a feature includes the effect of its interactions with other features and cannot separate them from its own effect. If two features interact, shuffling either one lowers the score, so importances need not add up to the model's total performance.
The ranking can change with the scoring metric, particularly for imbalanced classification, where accuracy and F1-score can give different pictures of which features matter.

Scores computed on training data can reflect overfitting: a feature the model has memorised can look important even though it does not help on new data. Use held-out data, and repeat the shuffle to see how much the scores vary.

resources.title: Random Forests
resources.abstract: Random forests are a combination of tree predictors such that each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest. The generalization error for forests converges a.s. to a limit as the number of trees in the forest becomes large. The generalization error of a forest of tree classifiers depends on the strength of the individual trees in the forest and the correlation between them. Using a random selection of features to split each node yields error rates that compare favorably to Adaboost (Y. Freund & R. Schapire, Machine Learning: Proceedings of the Thirteenth International conference, ***, 148–156), but are more robust with respect to noise. Internal estimates monitor error, strength, and correlation and these are used to show the response to increasing the number of features used in the splitting. Internal estimates are also used to measure variable importance. These ideas are also applicable to regression.

resources.title: All Models are Wrong, but Many are Useful: Learning a Variable's Importance by Studying an Entire Class of Prediction Models Simultaneously
resources.abstract: Variable importance (VI) tools describe how much covariates contribute to a prediction model's accuracy. However, important variables for one well-performing model (for example, a linear model $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{T}β$ with a fixed coefficient vector $β$) may be unimportant for another model. In this paper, we propose model class reliance (MCR) as the range of VI values across all well-performing model in a prespecified class. Thus, MCR gives a more comprehensive description of importance by accounting for the fact that many prediction models, possibly of different parametric forms, may fit the data well. In the process of deriving MCR, we show several informative results for permutation-based VI estimates, based on the VI measures used in Random Forests. Specifically, we derive connections between permutation importance estimates for a single prediction model, U-statistics, conditional variable importance, conditional causal effects, and linear model coefficients. We then give probabilistic bounds for MCR, using a novel, generalizable technique. We apply MCR to a public data set of Broward County criminal records to study the reliance of recidivism prediction models on sex and race. In this application, MCR can be used to help inform VI for unknown, proprietary models.

resources.title: RANDOM FORESTS FOR CLASSIFICATION IN ECOLOGY
resources.abstract: Classification procedures are some of the most widely used statistical methods in ecology. Random forests (RF) is a new and powerful statistical classifier that is well established in other disciplines but is relatively unknown in ecology. Advantages of RF compared to other statistical classifiers include (1) very high classification accuracy; (2) a novel method of determining variable importance; (3) ability to model complex interactions among predictor variables; (4) flexibility to perform several types of statistical data analysis, including regression, classification, survival analysis, and unsupervised learning; and (5) an algorithm for imputing missing values. We compared the accuracies of RF and four other commonly used statistical classifiers using data on invasive plant species presence in Lava Beds National Monument, California, USA, rare lichen species presence in the Pacific Northwest, USA, and nest sites for cavity nesting birds in the Uinta Mountains, Utah, USA. We observed high classification accuracy in all applications as measured by cross-validation and, in the case of the lichen data, by independent test data, when comparing RF to other common classification methods. We also observed that the variables that RF identified as most important for classifying invasive plant species coincided with expectations based on the literature.

techniques.name: Mean Decrease Impurity
techniques.description: Mean Decrease Impurity (MDI) scores how much each feature contributes to a tree-based model, such as a random forest, by looking at how the model's decision trees split the training data. Each split sends cases into two groups, and a good split makes each group more uniform in its outcome, which is a drop in impurity, measured with a score such as Gini impurity. For each feature, MDI adds up the drops from every split that uses it, weights each by the share of training cases reaching that split, and averages over all trees. The scores are usually scaled to sum to one, so they show relative importance. Because they come from the training data, they describe how the model was built, not how well each feature predicts on new data.

example_use_cases.description: Determining the most influential genetic markers in a decision tree model predicting disease susceptibility, by identifying which markers consistently lead to the purest splits between healthy and diseased patient groups.

A model-validation team reviews a gradient-boosted loan-default model and ranks its inputs by MDI before sign-off. They investigate any identifier-like or many-valued field, such as customer ID or postcode, that ranks near the top, because MDI favours such fields and they may reflect overfitting rather than real predictive signal.

An environmental analytics team fits a random forest to forecast air quality and uses MDI to choose which weather stations' readings to drop from a simpler model. They then confirm on held-out data that accuracy holds, because MDI alone reflects the training data.

limitations.description: MDI favours features with many distinct values, because more possible split points give more chances of a good split by chance. Strobl and colleagues found that uninformative continuous or many-category variables were preferred over informative ones when predictors differed in type or number of categories.

Scores are calculated from the training data, so a feature can rank high because the model fitted noise in it. A high score does not show that the feature helps predictions on unseen data, and scikit-learn recommends permutation importance on held-out data as the alternative.

MDI gives only a non-negative score for each feature. It does not show whether higher values of a feature raise or lower the prediction, so it cannot support a claim about the direction of a feature's effect.

Scores vary from tree to tree, and the scikit-learn example plots this spread as error bars. A forest with few trees, or a small training set, can therefore give a ranking that shifts when the model is refitted.
Correlated predictors compete for splits. One can mask another's importance, and changing the fitted ensemble or candidate-feature settings can change their relative ranks.

resources.title: Bias in random forest variable importance measures: Illustrations, sources and a solution
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Variable importance measures for random forests have been receiving increased attention as a means of variable selection in many classification tasks in bioinformatics and related scientific fields, for instance to select a subset of genetic markers relevant for the prediction of a certain disease. We show that random forest variable importance measures are a sensible means for variable selection in many applications, but are not reliable in situations where potential predictor variables vary in their scale of measurement or their number of categories. This is particularly important in genomics and computational biology, where predictors often include variables of different types, for example when predictors include both sequence data and continuous variables such as folding energy, or when amino acid sequence data show different numbers of categories. RESULTS: Simulation studies are presented illustrating that, when random forest variable importance measures are used with data of varying types, the results are misleading because suboptimal predictor variables may be artificially preferred in variable selection. The two mechanisms underlying this deficiency are biased variable selection in the individual classification trees used to build the random forest on one hand, and effects induced by bootstrap sampling with replacement on the other hand. CONCLUSION: We propose to employ an alternative implementation of random forests, that provides unbiased variable selection in the individual classification trees. When this method is applied using subsampling without replacement, the resulting variable importance measures can be used reliably for variable selection even in situations where the potential predictor variables vary in their scale of measurement or their number of categories. The usage of both random forest algorithms and their variable importance measures in the R system for statistical computing is illustrated and documented thoroughly in an application re-analyzing data from a study on RNA editing. Therefore the suggested method can be applied straightforwardly by scientists in bioinformatics research.

resources.title: A comparison of random forest and its Gini importance with standard chemometric methods for the feature selection and classification of spectral data
resources.abstract: Background Regularized regression methods such as principal component or partial least squares regression perform well in learning tasks on high dimensional spectral data, but cannot explicitly eliminate irrelevant features. The random forest classifier with its associated Gini feature importance, on the other hand, allows for an explicit feature elimination, but may not be optimally adapted to spectral data due to the topology of its constituent classification trees which are based on orthogonal splits in feature space. Results We propose to combine the best of both approaches, and evaluated the joint use of a feature selection based on a recursive feature elimination using the Gini importance of random forests' together with regularized classification methods on spectral data sets from medical diagnostics, chemotaxonomy, biomedical analytics, food science, and synthetically modified spectral data. Here, a feature selection using the Gini feature importance with a regularized classification by discriminant partial least squares regression performed as well as or better than a filtering according to different univariate statistical tests, or using regression coefficients in a backward feature elimination. It outperformed the direct application of the random forest classifier, or the direct application of the regularized classifiers on the full set of features. Conclusion The Gini importance of the random forest provided superior means for measuring feature relevance on spectral data, but – on an optimal subset of features – the regularized classifiers might be preferable over the random forest classifier, in spite of their limitation to model linear dependencies only. A feature selection based on Gini importance, however, may precede a regularized linear classification to identify this optimal subset of features, and to earn a double benefit of both dimensionality reduction and the elimination of noise from the classification task.

techniques.name: Coefficient Magnitudes (in Linear Models)
techniques.description: Coefficient Magnitudes explains a linear model by reading its fitted coefficients. Each coefficient shows how much the prediction changes when its feature rises by one unit while every other feature stays fixed, and its sign gives the direction. Because a coefficient's size depends on the units of its feature, the features are first put on a common scale, for example by standardising them or by multiplying each coefficient by its feature's standard deviation. The features with the largest scaled coefficients are then read as having the strongest influence on the model's predictions. This gives a global view of the model without needing a separate explanation method.

example_use_cases.description: An estate agency's data team standardises the inputs of a linear house-price model, then ranks the absolute coefficients to show valuers which property attributes move the estimate most. Valuers check that the signs match their experience, for example that more floor area raises the price, before the model guides asking prices.

A lender's model-risk team documents a linear credit-scoring model for its regulator by publishing the standardised coefficient of every input. The reviewer can read off the direction and relative weight of each input without a separate explanation tool, and can query any input that carries more weight than policy allows.

A public health analyst fits a logistic regression to predict emergency readmission and reports standardised coefficients to clinicians, who see which patient characteristics push the predicted risk up or down. The analyst refits on resamples first, to check that the large coefficients keep their sign.

limitations.description: Raw magnitudes have output-per-input units and cannot be ranked across differently scaled variables. Express comparable input changes explicitly; changing metres to centimetres makes the corresponding coefficient smaller for the same predictions.

Coefficients concern the encoded model inputs while other inputs are held fixed. If the model includes transformed variables or interactions, inspecting one coefficient does not give the whole effect of changing an original variable.

Correlated predictors can have unstable or shared coefficients even when predictions change little. Scaling does not remove this problem, and regularisation can change which correlated feature receives a large weight.

Each coefficient is conditional on the other features in the model. A feature can have a negative coefficient while rising with the outcome on its own, so a coefficient read in isolation can mislead about the feature's plain relationship to the outcome.

A coefficient is a conditional association in the fitted model, not a causal effect. Its magnitude alone also does not give a particular applicant's contribution, which depends on that applicant's feature values.

techniques.name: Integrated Gradients
techniques.description: Integrated Gradients assigns input features scores for a prediction relative to a chosen reference input, called the baseline. It evaluates gradients, rates of output change, at points along a straight path from that reference to the actual input. Each feature's average gradient is multiplied by its change from the reference, and the resulting scores sum approximately to the output difference when enough numerical steps are used. For text, the path runs through continuous token representations rather than discrete word identifiers, and scores can be combined into highlighted words. In a protected-term variant, the reviewer fixes before the run a list of words or columns that name or record a protected characteristic, and reads the scores those inputs receive: a large score shows that the output rests partly on the characteristic, but a small score does not show that the model ignores it.

example_use_cases.description: An eye-screening programme evaluating a diabetic retinopathy grading model shows graders an Integrated Gradients heatmap beside each prediction, so they can see whether the regions driving a referral are lesions such as haemorrhages rather than camera artefacts, and uses the review to decide whether the model may assist grading.

A team building a question-answering assistant over an organisation's policy documents attributes each answer to the question's tokens and flags questions where the content words receive almost no attribution; those questions become test cases in which the content words are changed, to show whether the assistant actually reads the question.

A trust-and-safety team reviewing the posts its toxic-content classifier wrongly flagged fixes, before the run, a list of identity terms (names of religions, ethnicities and sexual orientations, chosen because the policy forbids penalising them) and computes Integrated Gradients against an all-padding baseline. Where a listed term ranks among the five most attributed tokens of a wrongly flagged post, the team adds counter-examples to the training data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A lender's model-risk team audits a classifier that reads the free-text statements in loan applications. Before the run it lists the words that state a protected characteristic, such as a religion, a pregnancy or a disability, and computes Integrated Gradients against a documented reference statement for a sample of declined applications. Any listed word among the ten most attributed is reported for a swap test; the absence of such words does not show the model ignores them.

limitations.description: Attributions are measured against the baseline and no choice is neutral. Features that match the baseline score near zero even when the model relies on them: with a black-image baseline, dark pixels on the object get little credit. A comparison of blurred, noise and training-data baselines found none best, so the baseline is an assumption to state and to vary before drawing conclusions.

Requires gradient access to a differentiable model, so it cannot explain tree ensembles, rule-based components or a model reached only through an API. For text, the path runs through token embeddings whose intermediate points are not real words, and subword tokenisation splits a word across several scores that must be recombined before a reviewer can read them.

Each explanation needs one gradient computation per step along the path; the original authors found 20 to 300 steps were usually enough for the scores to sum to within 5% of the output difference. Explaining long documents, high-resolution images or a large audit sample therefore costs tens to hundreds of forward and backward passes per prediction.

A score shows how sensitive the output was to a feature along one straight path, not that the feature causes the outcome in the world or that removing it would change the decision. Maps over neighbouring pixels or tokens are often noisy, and a plausible-looking heatmap does not show that the model's reasoning is sound.

resources.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
resources.abstract: We study the problem of attributing the prediction of a deep network to its input features, a problem previously studied by several other works. We identify two fundamental axioms---Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance that attribution methods ought to satisfy. We show that they are not satisfied by most known attribution methods, which we consider to be a fundamental weakness of those methods. We use the axioms to guide the design of a new attribution method called Integrated Gradients. Our method requires no modification to the original network and is extremely simple to implement; it just needs a few calls to the standard gradient operator. We apply this method to a couple of image models, a couple of text models and a chemistry model, demonstrating its ability to debug networks, to extract rules from a network, and to enable users to engage with models better.

resources.title: Using a Deep Learning Algorithm and Integrated Gradients Explanation to Assist Grading for Diabetic Retinopathy
resources.abstract: PURPOSE: To understand the impact of deep learning diabetic retinopathy (DR) algorithms on physician readers in computer-assisted settings. DESIGN: Evaluation of diagnostic technology. PARTICIPANTS: One thousand seven hundred ninety-six retinal fundus images from 1612 diabetic patients. METHODS: Ten ophthalmologists (5 general ophthalmologists, 4 retina specialists, 1 retina fellow) read images for DR severity based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy disease severity scale in each of 3 conditions: unassisted, grades only, or grades plus heatmap. Grades-only assistance comprised a histogram of DR predictions (grades) from a trained deep-learning model. For grades plus heatmap, we additionally showed explanatory heatmaps. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: For each experiment arm, we computed sensitivity and specificity of each reader and the algorithm for different levels of DR severity against an adjudicated reference standard. We also measured accuracy (exact 5-class level agreement and Cohen's quadratically weighted κ), reader-reported confidence (5-point Likert scale), and grading time. RESULTS: Readers graded more accurately with model assistance than without for the grades-only condition (P < 0.001). Grades plus heatmaps improved accuracy for patients with DR (P < 0.001), but reduced accuracy for patients without DR (P = 0.006). Both forms of assistance increased readers' sensitivity moderate-or-worse DR: unassisted: mean, 79.4% [95% confidence interval (CI), 72.3%-86.5%]; grades only: mean, 87.5% [95% CI, 85.1%-89.9%]; grades plus heatmap: mean, 88.7% [95% CI, 84.9%-92.5%] without a corresponding drop in specificity (unassisted: mean, 96.6% [95% CI, 95.9%-97.4%]; grades only: mean, 96.1% [95% CI, 95.5%-96.7%]; grades plus heatmap: mean, 95.5% [95% CI, 94.8%-96.1%]). Algorithmic assistance increased the accuracy of retina specialists above that of the unassisted reader or model alone; and increased grading confidence and grading time across all readers. For most cases, grades plus heatmap was only as effective as grades only. Over the course of the experiment, grading time decreased across all conditions, although most sharply for grades plus heatmap. CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning algorithms can improve the accuracy of, and confidence in, DR diagnosis in an assisted read setting. They also may increase grading time, although these effects may be ameliorated with experience.

techniques.name: DeepLIFT
techniques.description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group training a neural network to predict where a regulatory protein binds DNA computes DeepLIFT scores for each predicted binding region against a reference sequence with background base frequencies. They read off which short stretches of bases carry the score, compare them with known binding motifs, and decide whether the model has learned real regulatory sequence before using it to prioritise experiments.

A hospital imaging team is investigating a chest X-ray classifier that flags healthy patients as abnormal. For the false positives it computes DeepLIFT scores against a blurred copy of each image and checks whether the weight sits on the image border, where scanner labels are printed, rather than on lung tissue. It then decides whether to mask the labels and retrain.

A regional geohazard agency uses a neural network to rate landslide susceptibility from terrain, rainfall and land-cover layers. For a slope the model rates as high risk, DeepLIFT scores show which input layers drove the rating, and the agency compares them with the field investigation report before using the map for planning.

A lender's credit team sends each declined applicant a short statement of the factors that most lowered their score. For its neural network scorer it computes DeepLIFT scores against a documented reference applicant, the median approved applicant, and the statement lists the factors with the largest negative scores, which are the ones that pulled this score below the reference.

limitations.description: Every score is relative to a reference input, and the choice changes the picture. In the original paper an all-zero reference on CIFAR-10 images highlighted hard-to-interpret background pixels, while a blurred copy of the image highlighted object outlines. State the reference used and repeat the analysis with at least one alternative before drawing conclusions.

The Captum implementation supports only the Rescale rule, which can give all the credit to one of two inputs that jointly drive the output. In the paper's min(i1, i2) example Rescale scores only the smaller input, while the RevealCancel rule shares the credit. Where inputs interact, the scores can hide a dependency that a more complete rule would show.

Propagation rules must support the network operations. Captum implements the Rescale rule and a limited set of nonlinearities; inaccessible operations in built-in recurrent modules can prevent attribution unless a supported implementation is used.

Two networks that compute exactly the same function can receive different DeepLIFT scores, because differences between a neuron and its reference do not obey the chain rule that gradients obey (Sundararajan et al., 2017, App. B). The scores therefore describe how the model is built as well as what it computes, which matters when comparing a model with a re-implemented or compressed version of it.

Feature contributions account for a particular output difference, not a causal effect in the world or a guaranteed change after deleting that feature. Correlated genomic bases or financial variables make that distinction important.

resources.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
resources.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

resources.title: An Attribution Deep Learning Interpretation Model for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) due to their higher accuracy. However, due to the lack of explanations of the influence of input contributing factors by current DL models, accurately identifying the cause of each landslide remains challenging. This study proposes a novel interpretable DL model named Deep-Attention-LSF, which assigns significance scores to contributing factors at local levels for attributing landslide susceptibility. This model considers the significance scores of input factors to more accurately predict landslide occurrence. DeepLIFT is used as an attribution branching network for interpreting the relationship between input factors and each landslide event. Subsequently, a landslide classification network formed by combining convolutional neural network and long short-term memory is used to predict the landslide occurrence in the entire study area. The performance of Deep-Attention-LSF is tested using the landslide inventory map of Three Gorges reservoir area and the associated maps of 18 landslide-related factors. The accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score of our model were 0.9645, 0.9583, 0.9676, and 0.9522, respectively. These suggest that our model outperformed the compared models, including self-attention LSM, frequency-ratio-attention LSM, bagging and random subspace naive bayes tree, gradient boosting decision tree, random forest, information value model and enhanced C5.0 decision tree model. Deep-Attention-LSF provided reasonable explanations for landslide attributions by comparison with field investigation reports for four specific landslide cases. Combining the interpretation of Deep-Attention-LSF with field investigations can provide more comprehensive information for evaluating specific landslides, providing a useful tool for landslide prevention and management.

techniques.name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
techniques.description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which pixels in chest X-rays contribute to pneumonia detection, helping radiologists verify AI diagnoses by highlighting anatomical regions the model considers relevant.

A perception team investigating a misclassified traffic-sign image draws the relevance map for the wrong class. The map shows the relevance sitting on a sticker and the background rather than on the sign itself, which tells the team to add training images with such clutter before the model is retested.

A bank's model-risk reviewers receive LRP relevance scores for a sample of declined applications scored by a neural network. They check that the inputs with the most relevance for the decline output are affordability measures and not proxy fields such as postcode, and file the scores with the decision record for audit.

limitations.description: Each layer type needs its own propagation rule, and a new layer type has none until someone derives one, so adapting LRP to a new architecture takes expertise and testing.
Rule selection (LRP-ε, LRP-γ and others) changes the resulting maps, so two analysts can produce different explanations of the same prediction, and choosing among them takes expertise.

Heatmaps are hard to validate. The original paper judges them by eye and with a pixel-flipping test, and notes that quality beyond visual assessment is an open question, so a plausible-looking map does not prove the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Standard rules do not cover attention layers. Extensions for transformers, such as AttnLRP in the LXT library, exist but are recent and specific to certain architectures, so users of transformers or large language models must adopt them and confirm they match their model.

Bias handling and epsilon stabilisation can absorb or inject relevance, so input scores do not always sum exactly to the selected output. A report should document the accounting residual before claiming conservation.

resources.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
resources.abstract: Understanding and interpreting classification decisions of automated image classification systems is of high value in many applications, as it allows to verify the reasoning of the system and provides additional information to the human expert. Although machine learning methods are solving very successfully a plethora of tasks, they have in most cases the disadvantage of acting as a black box, not providing any information about what made them arrive at a particular decision. This work proposes a general solution to the problem of understanding classification decisions by pixel-wise decomposition of nonlinear classifiers. We introduce a methodology that allows to visualize the contributions of single pixels to predictions for kernel-based classifiers over Bag of Words features and for multilayered neural networks. These pixel contributions can be visualized as heatmaps and are provided to a human expert who can intuitively not only verify the validity of the classification decision, but also focus further analysis on regions of potential interest. We evaluate our method for classifiers trained on PASCAL VOC 2009 images, synthetic image data containing geometric shapes, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and for the pre-trained ImageNet model available as part of the Caffe open source package.

resources.title: Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Explaining Deep Neural Network Decisions in MRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks have led to state-of-the-art results in many medical imaging tasks including Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, the network decisions are often perceived as being highly non-transparent, making it difficult to apply these algorithms in clinical routine. In this study, we propose using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to visualize convolutional neural network decisions for AD based on MRI data. Similarly to other visualization methods, LRP produces a heatmap in the input space indicating the importance/relevance of each voxel contributing to the final classification outcome. In contrast to susceptibility maps produced by guided backpropagation ("Which change in voxels would change the outcome most?"), the LRP method is able to directly highlight positive contributions to the network classification in the input space. In particular, we show that (1) the LRP method is very specific for individuals ("Why does this person have AD?") with high inter-patient variability, (2) there is very little relevance for AD in healthy controls and (3) areas that exhibit a lot of relevance correlate well with what is known from literature. To quantify the latter, we compute size-corrected metrics of the summed relevance per brain area, e.g., relevance density or relevance gain. Although these metrics produce very individual "fingerprints" of relevance patterns for AD patients, a lot of importance is put on areas in the temporal lobe including the hippocampus. After discussing several limitations such as sensitivity toward the underlying model and computation parameters, we conclude that LRP might have a high potential to assist clinicians in explaining neural network decisions for diagnosing AD (and potentially other diseases) based on structural MRI data.

techniques.name: Contextual Decomposition
techniques.description: Contextual Decomposition explains why an LSTM, a neural network that reads text one word at a time, made a particular prediction. The user picks a word or phrase, and the method splits the network's output score into two parts: the part due to that phrase alone, and the part due to everything else, including how the phrase interacts with the words around it. Comparing a phrase's score with the scores of its parts reveals effects that word-by-word methods miss, such as a negation reversing the sentiment of the word that follows it. The split is tracked through the LSTM's internal gates, so the model itself is not changed or retrained. The output is a numerical score for each phrase examined.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing why an LSTM-based spam filter flagged an email by decomposing contributions from individual words ('free', 'urgent') versus their contextual interactions ('free trial' together).

A hospital analytics team checks an LSTM that flags clinical notes mentioning possible pneumonia. Contextual decomposition shows whether negated findings such as 'no evidence of pneumonia' push the score down, as intended, or whether the model reacts to the word 'pneumonia' alone, which tells the team if it needs retraining on negated examples before use.

A platform's trust-and-safety team handles an appeal against an LSTM toxicity classifier's removal of a post. The reviewing moderator is shown the phrases with the highest contextual decomposition scores, including whether a negation such as 'not stupid' was read correctly, so the moderator can judge whether the removal rested on the post's actual meaning.

limitations.description: Developed for LSTMs, whose gates the method uses to separate a phrase's own effect from its interactions. The source does not cover plain recurrent networks, transformers or attention models, so teams using those cannot apply the published method as it stands.
Needs internal states, gate parameters and classifier weights. Output labels or probabilities alone do not reveal the phrase-related and remaining-input components.

The user must choose each phrase to examine, and the published method handles contiguous phrases. The number of possible phrases grows quickly with text length, so scanning a whole document for interactions is costly and easy to leave incomplete.

The split relies on linearising the gate and activation functions and averaging over orderings of the terms. Interaction scores are therefore approximate, and the source validates them only on sentiment tasks (Stanford Sentiment Treebank, Yelp), so scores on other tasks need checking independently.

Components combine additively in hidden states and class scores before the probability transformation. They should not be read as independent probabilities or as the exact effect of deleting a phrase.

resources.title: Beyond Word Importance: Contextual Decomposition to Extract Interactions from LSTMs
resources.abstract: The driving force behind the recent success of LSTMs has been their ability to learn complex and non-linear relationships. Consequently, our inability to describe these relationships has led to LSTMs being characterized as black boxes. To this end, we introduce contextual decomposition (CD), an interpretation algorithm for analysing individual predictions made by standard LSTMs, without any changes to the underlying model. By decomposing the output of a LSTM, CD captures the contributions of combinations of words or variables to the final prediction of an LSTM. On the task of sentiment analysis with the Yelp and SST data sets, we show that CD is able to reliably identify words and phrases of contrasting sentiment, and how they are combined to yield the LSTM's final prediction. Using the phrase-level labels in SST, we also demonstrate that CD is able to successfully extract positive and negative negations from an LSTM, something which has not previously been done.

resources.title: Interpreting patient-Specific risk prediction using contextual decomposition of BiLSTMs: Application to children with asthma
resources.abstract: Background Predictive modeling with longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data offers great promise for accelerating personalized medicine and better informs clinical decision-making. Recently, deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance for many healthcare prediction tasks. However, deep models lack interpretability, which is integral to successful decision-making and can lead to better patient care. In this paper, we build upon the contextual decomposition (CD) method, an algorithm for producing importance scores from long short-term memory networks (LSTMs). We extend the method to bidirectional LSTMs (BiLSTMs) and use it in the context of predicting future clinical outcomes using patients’ EHR historical visits. Methods We use a real EHR dataset comprising 11071 patients, to evaluate and compare CD interpretations from LSTM and BiLSTM models. First, we train LSTM and BiLSTM models for the task of predicting which pre-school children with respiratory system-related complications will have asthma at school-age. After that, we conduct quantitative and qualitative analysis to evaluate the CD interpretations produced by the contextual decomposition of the trained models. In addition, we develop an interactive visualization to demonstrate the utility of CD scores in explaining predicted outcomes. Results Our experimental evaluation demonstrate that whenever a clear visit-level pattern exists, the models learn that pattern and the contextual decomposition can appropriately attribute the prediction to the correct pattern. In addition, the results confirm that the CD scores agree to a large extent with the importance scores generated using logistic regression coefficients. Our main insight was that rather than interpreting the attribution of individual visits to the predicted outcome, we could instead attribute a model’s prediction to a group of visits. Conclusion We presented a quantitative and qualitative evidence that CD interpretations can explain patient-specific predictions using CD attributions of individual visits or a group of visits.

In the news-sentiment model used for credit monitoring, the contribution of a sentiment word changes sign when a negation or contrast precedes it, and contextual decomposition separates the word's own effect from its context.

For the audited support tickets, the routing model's decision is not driven by any single trigger word: phrase-level contextual decomposition scores account for more of the output than the strongest single-word score.

techniques.name: Taylor Decomposition
techniques.description: Taylor Decomposition explains one prediction of a neural network by splitting its output score into a contribution from each input, such as each pixel. It starts from a reference input, called a root point, that is close to the real input but for which the network's score is zero. Each input's contribution is the slope of the score with respect to that input at the root point, multiplied by how far the input sits from the root, and terms that involve several inputs at once are left out. Finding a good root point is slow for large networks, so the deep variant applies the same idea to one neuron at a time and passes the contributions backwards through the layers, which gives rules close to those of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation. The result is a relevance score for every input that can be drawn as a heatmap.

example_use_cases.description: A quality team uses a convolutional network to flag defective printed circuit boards. For each flagged board they draw the deep Taylor heatmap and check that the highlighted pixels sit on the defect and not on a board label, the edge or the background, before they trust the flags enough to stop manual inspection.

A hospital's model-validation group audits a ReLU network that classifies chest X-rays. For a sample of positive cases, deep Taylor relevance shows whether the evidence for the finding lies inside the lungs or on markers, text or borders added by the imaging equipment, before the group signs the model off for a pilot.

A bank's data science team has a ReLU network that scores small-business loan applications from tabular inputs. For a declined application, deep Taylor relevance lists which inputs supplied most of the score, so a reviewer can see whether the decision rests on repayment history and income or on a field such as postcode.

limitations.description: The explanation depends on the choice of root point, and different reference inputs give different attributions. Finding the nearest root needs an iterative optimisation that is slow for large networks and may not converge, which is why the source applies the deep variant to large image networks.

Plain Taylor decomposition uses only first-order terms, so joint effects of several inputs stay unattributed and the scores need not add up to the prediction. In the source's tests the nearest-root version lost a large share of the relevance, so its heatmaps can leave much of the prediction unexplained.

The deep variant's guarantees, scores that add up to the prediction and are never negative, are proved for ReLU-style layers with zero or negative biases, and iNNvestigate documents support for ReLU networks only. Other activations, positive biases or normalisation layers need workarounds that the proofs do not cover.

Heatmaps explain one input at a time and are hard to validate. The source judges them by eye and by checking that relevance is conserved on MNIST digits and ImageNet photos, so a plausible-looking map does not prove that the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Requires access to internal layer operations and supported redistribution rules. A prediction-only service cannot supply this layer-wise decomposition, and an image-derived rule should not be assumed valid for arbitrary text or attention models.

resources.title: Explaining NonLinear Classification Decisions with Deep Taylor Decomposition
resources.abstract: Nonlinear methods such as Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are the gold standard for various challenging machine learning problems, e.g., image classification, natural language processing or human action recognition. Although these methods perform impressively well, they have a significant disadvantage, the lack of transparency, limiting the interpretability of the solution and thus the scope of application in practice. Especially DNNs act as black boxes due to their multilayer nonlinear structure. In this paper we introduce a novel methodology for interpreting generic multilayer neural networks by decomposing the network classification decision into contributions of its input elements. Although our focus is on image classification, the method is applicable to a broad set of input data, learning tasks and network architectures. Our method is based on deep Taylor decomposition and efficiently utilizes the structure of the network by backpropagating the explanations from the output to the input layer. We evaluate the proposed method empirically on the MNIST and ILSVRC data sets.

techniques.name: Sobol Indices
techniques.description: Sobol indices show how much of the variation in a model's output can be traced to each of its inputs. The analyst sets a range or probability distribution for every input and runs the model on a large, carefully designed sample of input combinations. The variance (spread) of the outputs is then split into shares. A first-order index is the share caused by one input varying on its own, and a total-order index also counts every interaction that input takes part in. A large gap between the two signals that an input matters mainly through interactions, and optional second-order indices show which pairs of inputs interact.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing a climate prediction model to determine which atmospheric parameters (temperature, humidity, pressure) contribute most to rainfall forecast uncertainty, helping meteorologists understand which measurements need the highest precision.

A risk team validating a portfolio valuation model asks which economic indicators (interest rates, inflation, GDP growth) drive most of the variation in predicted portfolio value. A large gap between an indicator's total-order and first-order indices shows it acts mainly through interactions, which tells the team which scenarios to stress-test together.

limitations.description: The standard sampling scheme needs N(2D+2) model runs for D inputs (N(D+2) without second-order indices), with N often in the thousands. A slow model, or one with dozens of inputs, quickly becomes impractical. Grouping related inputs, or screening first with a cheaper method such as Morris, reduces the cost.

Assumes the inputs vary independently. If real inputs are correlated, for example income and postcode, the sample contains combinations the model never meets in practice, and the indices can mislead about which inputs matter.

Needs a probability distribution or range for every input, and the indices depend on that choice, because widening one input's range raises its share of the variance. If the ranges do not reflect the real deployment population, the ranking describes a model the users will never face.

Variance is the only yardstick. When the output is heavily skewed or has several peaks, variance shares can be unreliable guides to which inputs matter, and a moment-independent method such as PAWN may suit better.

Estimates carry sampling error. With too few runs the confidence intervals can be as wide as the indices themselves, so small indices cannot be told apart from zero. Report the intervals SALib returns and check that the ranking holds when N is increased.

resources.abstract: Feature selection (FS) is vitally important for determining the optimum subsets of features with effective information and maximizing the model accuracy. This study proposes a novel FS method based on global sensitivity analysis (GSA) for effectively determining the most relevant feature subsets and improving prediction performance of machine learning (ML)based models. Feature ranking is determined based on the results obtained from three global sensitivity analysis (GSA) including Pearson, Sobol’ and PAWN. This novel GSA-based FS method is applied to engineering practice with the combination of ML algorithm random forest (RF) to predict tunnelling-induced settlement prediction model. Meanwhile, the feature extraction method principle component analysis (PCA) is also used to develop RF-based model for comparing the performance of proposed GSA-based FS method. The results indicate the novel GSA-based FS method effectively determines the significance of input variables. The prediction performance of RF-based model with the integration of GSA-based FS methods is enhanced dramatically, and obviously outperforms the model with the integration of PCA-based dimensionality reduction method.

techniques.name: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
techniques.description: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) explains individual predictions by approximating the complex model's behaviour in a small neighbourhood around a specific instance. It works by creating perturbed versions of the input (e.g., removing words from text, changing pixel values in images, or varying feature values), obtaining the model's predictions for these variations, and training a simple interpretable model (typically linear regression) weighted by proximity to the original instance. The coefficients of this local surrogate model reveal which features most influenced the specific prediction.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining why a specific patient received a high-risk diagnosis by showing which symptoms (fever, blood pressure, age) contributed most to the prediction, helping doctors validate the AI's reasoning.
Debugging a text classifier's misclassification of a movie review by highlighting which words (e.g., sarcastic phrases) confused the model, enabling targeted model improvements.

Showing insurance customers the claim features that most influenced an automated approval or denial. A reviewer first checks that the explanation is stable across repeated runs and plausible for that claim, because it approximates the model locally and may not match its full reasoning.

limitations.description: Explanations can be unstable due to random sampling, producing different results across multiple runs.
The linear surrogate may poorly approximate highly non-linear model behaviour in the local region.
Defining the neighbourhood size and perturbation strategy requires careful tuning for each data type.
Can be computationally expensive for explaining many instances due to repeated model queries.

Assumes features are independent when generating perturbations, producing unrealistic out-of-distribution samples for datasets with correlated features. This can generate misleading attribution scores when inputs share strong correlations (e.g., age and income in credit scoring, comorbidities in clinical data).

resources.title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
resources.abstract: Despite widespread adoption, machine learning models remain mostly black boxes. Understanding the reasons behind predictions is, however, quite important in assessing trust, which is fundamental if one plans to take action based on a prediction, or when choosing whether to deploy a new model. Such understanding also provides insights into the model, which can be used to transform an untrustworthy model or prediction into a trustworthy one. In this work, we propose LIME, a novel explanation technique that explains the predictions of any classifier in an interpretable and faithful manner, by learning an interpretable model locally around the prediction. We also propose a method to explain models by presenting representative individual predictions and their explanations in a non-redundant way, framing the task as a submodular optimization problem. We demonstrate the flexibility of these methods by explaining different models for text (e.g. random forests) and image classification (e.g. neural networks). We show the utility of explanations via novel experiments, both simulated and with human subjects, on various scenarios that require trust: deciding if one should trust a prediction, choosing between models, improving an untrustworthy classifier, and identifying why a classifier should not be trusted.

resources.title: Lime — basic usage, two class case (lime project tutorial)
Evaluating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations on Clinical Machine Learning Classification Models
resources.abstract: The usage of black-box classification models within the healthcare field is highly dependent on being interpretable by the receiver. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanation (LIME) provides a patient-specific explanation for a given classification, thus enhancing the possibility for any complex classifier to serve as a safety aid within a clinical setting. However, research on if the explanation provided by LIME is relevant to clinicians is limited and there is no current framework for how an evaluation of LIME is to be performed. To evaluate the clinical relevance of the explanations provided by LIME, this study has investigated how physician's independent explanations for classified observations compare with explanations provided by LIME. Additionally, the clinical relevance and the experienced reliance on the explanations provided by LIME have been evaluated by field experts. techniques.name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
techniques.description: A ridge regression surrogate approximates a complex model with a linear equation fitted to the complex model's own predictions. The complex model is run on a set of inputs, and ridge regression, a linear model with a penalty that keeps coefficients stable when features are correlated, is fitted to reproduce its outputs. Each coefficient then shows roughly how far a feature moves the complex model's output, averaged over those inputs. Fidelity, often reported as R-squared (the share of the model's variation the surrogate reproduces on held-out inputs), shows how far the coefficients can be trusted. They describe the complex model, not the real world.

example_use_cases.description: A model-risk team at a bank fits a ridge surrogate to a gradient-boosted credit-scoring model's scores on a held-out sample, reports how closely the surrogate reproduces them, and uses the standardised coefficients to brief the model-risk committee on which inputs drive scores overall.

A hospital analytics team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural network that predicts readmission risk from tabular records, to check that the features driving the network's predictions overall, such as age and prior admissions, are plausible to clinicians. The findings concern the network, not what causes readmission.

An energy company's forecasting team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural-network load forecaster using a year of hourly weather and calendar inputs, and reads the standardised coefficients to confirm that temperature and time of day dominate. A low R-squared during heatwaves leads the team to record that the surrogate does not describe the model in that regime.

An insurer's compliance team gives a regulator a ridge surrogate of its pricing model together with held-out R-squared and a table of each feature's contribution to a sample of quotes, so the regulator can check the stated drivers against the model's actual outputs.

limitations.description: A linear surrogate cannot represent interactions or thresholds. Where the complex model relies on them, the surrogate fits its predictions poorly and its coefficients describe a different model. Report held-out R-squared and treat a low value as a failed surrogate.

A good average fit can hide poor fit in parts of the input space, such as rare groups or extreme values, so the coefficients may be wrong for exactly the cases that matter. Check fidelity within subgroups and near decision boundaries.
There is no agreed fidelity level above which a surrogate can be trusted. Whether 50%, 80% or 99% of variance explained is enough depends on the use, so the reviewer has to set and justify a cut-off.

Ridge shrinks every coefficient and shares weight between correlated features. Coefficient sizes depend on the penalty strength and on feature scaling, so compare them only after standardising the features, and report the penalty used.

The surrogate explains the complex model's behaviour on the sampled inputs, not the real-world link between features and outcomes. Reading its coefficients as causes, or as evidence about the data, will mislead.

techniques.name: Partial Dependence Plots
techniques.description: Partial Dependence Plots show how changing one or two features affects a model's predictions on average. The technique works by varying the selected feature(s) across their full range whilst keeping all other features fixed at their original values, then averaging the predictions. This creates a clear visualisation of whether increasing or decreasing a feature tends to increase or decrease predictions, and reveals patterns like linear trends, plateaus, or threshold effects that help explain model behaviour.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing how house prices change with property size in a real estate prediction model, revealing whether the relationship is linear or if there are diminishing returns for very large properties.
Examining how customer age affects predicted loan default probability in a credit scoring model, showing whether risk increases steadily with age or has specific age ranges with higher risk.
Visualising how temperature affects crop yield predictions in agricultural models, identifying optimal temperature ranges and potential threshold effects.

limitations.description: Assumes the plotted features are independent of the others. When they are correlated, the averaging pairs values that never occur together, so the curve partly reflects how the model behaves in regions with no data.

Shows only the average effect. If a feature acts in opposite directions for different groups of instances, the effects cancel and the curve can look flat, so interactions with other features stay hidden.
Limited to one or two features at a time, because higher-dimensional plots cannot be read. Effects that depend on three or more features together cannot be shown.
The basic method needs a pass over the whole dataset for every grid value, so cost grows with dataset size, the number of grid points and the time the model takes to predict.

resources.title: Using machine learning to examine freight network spatial vulnerabilities to disasters: A new take on partial dependence plots
resources.abstract: Analyzing transportation network vulnerabilities to disruptions is crucial for society to maintain commodity flows across the globe. However, most vulnerability analyses focus on impacts that arise from the deterioration of single network components, which can overlook spatial correlations between multiple components that manifest during area-spanning disruptions, such as those stemming from natural hazards. Here, we demonstrate an intuitive, simulation-based approach for inferring spatial vulnerabilities to area-spanning disruptions. In particular, we show how partial dependence plots derived from gradient boosting machines trained on the results of a routing simulation can be used to depict the average effect a disruption’s location has on impacts while controlling for other input variables and spatial dependencies embedded in the network. Although we demonstrate our approach for Middle Tennessee’s intermodal road and rail freight transportation network, our framework can easily be applied to other networks.

resources.title: Uncovering nonlinear patterns in time-sensitive prehospital breathing emergencies: an exploratory machine learning study
resources.abstract: Background Timely prehospital care is crucial for patients presenting with high-risk time-sensitive (HRTS) conditions. However, the interplay between response time and demographic factors in patients with breathing problems remains insufficiently understood. In this exploratory study, we applied machine learning (ML) to examine how emergency medical response time, age, and sex jointly influence the probability of encountering HRTS conditions. Methods A retrospective observational analysis was conducted on 132,395 prehospital missions in Stockholm (2017–2022). Multiple ML models, random forest, gradient boosting, neural networks, and logistic regression were trained to probe potential nonlinear patterns and interactions, not with the primary goal of predictive accuracy. Model performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC) measures. However, partial dependence (PD) and individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots were the principal tools illustrating how response time, age, and sex shape HRTS likelihood. Results PD and ICE plots revealed that older age (> 60 years) was consistently associated with a higher probability of HRTS. Moreover, patients over 60 years displayed a complex, rising risk at prolonged response times exceeding two hours. Gradient boosting offered the best (though modest) classification metrics, with an AUC of 0.66 and an F1-score of 0.55. We emphasize that these metrics, while necessary for completeness, were secondary to our aim of characterizing nonlinear relationships. Conclusions Our findings underscore the exploratory value of ML in identifying subtle relationships and interactions among response time, age, and sex for time-sensitive breathing emergencies. These results highlight opportunities to refine dispatch protocols, develop age- and sex-focused screening questions, and revisit lower-priority calls after extended wait times. Future work should incorporate richer data and refine these insights for potential predictive use. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

techniques.name: Individual Conditional Expectation Plots
techniques.description: Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots display the predicted output for individual instances as a function of a feature, with all other features held fixed for each instance. Each line on an ICE plot represents one instance's prediction trajectory as the feature of interest changes, revealing whether different instances are affected differently by that feature. This complements Partial Dependence Plots by showing heterogeneous effects across individual instances rather than just the average trend.

example_use_cases.description: A valuation team checks a house-price model before using it for automated estimates. ICE lines for property age show most homes losing value as they age, but a group of pre-1900 homes gaining value. The team asks whether the model has learned a real heritage premium or is reacting to a handful of unusual sales.

A hospital data science team reviews a diabetes risk model before clinicians use it. ICE lines of predicted risk against BMI rise steadily for most patients but stay flat for a small group. The team colours the lines by recorded characteristics, such as age band, to see what the flat group shares, then asks a clinician whether a flat response is plausible.

A credit risk validation team marks each applicant's actual income on that applicant's ICE line for a loan pricing model. For some applicant profiles the line changes steeply at incomes where no similar applicants appear in the training data. The team treats that part of the line as extrapolation and restricts the model's use to the supported range.

limitations.description: With hundreds or thousands of cases the lines overlap into a dense band that hides individual behaviour. Plotting a sample of lines, shifting them to start at the same point, or colouring them by a second feature is usually needed before the plot can be read.

Each line changes one feature while holding the case's other features fixed. Where features are correlated, parts of a line describe combinations that never occur in the data, so the model is extrapolating there. Marking each case's actual feature value on its line shows which part of the line the data supports.

Lines that are not parallel show that the feature's effect depends on other features, but not which ones. Finding out means colouring the lines by candidate features one at a time, so the search is by trial and error.

Judging whether lines differ by more than chance is done by eye, and a model can produce uneven lines from noise alone. The authors' formal check hides the real plot among plots made from additive fits, which needs the model to be refitted many times.

In its basic form the plot needs a model prediction for every case at every observed value of the feature, so the number of predictions grows with the square of the dataset size. Large datasets or slow models call for sampling.

resources.title: Peeking Inside the Black Box: Visualizing Statistical Learning with Plots of Individual Conditional Expectation
resources.abstract: This article presents Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots, a tool for visualizing the model estimated by any supervised learning algorithm. Classical partial dependence plots (PDPs) help visualize the average partial relationship between the predicted response and one or more features. In the presence of substantial interaction effects, the partial response relationship can be heterogeneous. Thus, an average curve, such as the PDP, can obfuscate the complexity of the modeled relationship. Accordingly, ICE plots refine the partial dependence plot by graphing the functional relationship between the predicted response and the feature for individual observations. Specifically, ICE plots highlight the variation in the fitted values across the range of a covariate, suggesting where and to what extent heterogeneities might exist. In addition to providing a plotting suite for exploratory analysis, we include a visual test for additive structure in the data generating model. Through simulated examples and real data sets, we demonstrate how ICE plots can shed light on estimated models in ways PDPs cannot. Procedures outlined are available in the R package ICEbox.
